item.title: The Army is testing self-driving vehicles at bases in Georgia and Texas
item.description:
Self-driving vehicle tests are planned for Fort Benning, Georgia and Fort Hood, Texas. Testing in Georgia began last week.

The post The Army is testing self-driving vehicles at bases in Georgia and Texas appeared first on Task & Purpose.
item.content:encoded:
The Army is looking to join the world of Waymo and Tesla Robotaxi, and take soldiers across base by self-driving car instead of having their peers shuttle them around to field exercises or other official duty events.

Officials at Fort Benning, Georgia, began testing several autonomous cars and vans as part of a pilot and larger Department of Defense effort to replace the military’s fleet of non-tactical vehicles used to move heavy supplies for field exercises, or transport troops for training or official ceremonies.

“Every day, thousands of initial-entry trainees, permanent-party cadre, and tenant unit soldiers move across Fort Benning’s expansive ranges, cantonment areas, and support facilities,” Charles Auer, head of the autonomous vehicle pilot at the Georgia base, said in a recent Army news release.

In May, the Army and the Defense Innovation Unit launched the Robotic Operation for Autonomous Delivery and Sustainment challenge, offering commercial companies up to $30 million in prizes to pitch autonomous options as replacements for the Defense Department’s fleet of more than 150,000 “non-tactical” vehicles like sedans, SUVs, trucks and vans. According to the innovation unit, the goal is to reduce the demand on military personnel (some of whom drive trucks as an assigned duty) and lower transportation costs.

“We want vehicles that let our soldiers operate more safely, more efficiently, and over time, give them more time to focus on core soldier activities other than driving water and MREs around post,” said Alex Miller, Chief Technology Officer for the Army Chief of Staff.

    By Patty Nieberg

  • News

    Family sues Air Force over daughter’s brain injury from birth overseas

    By Patty Nieberg

  • News

    Father shares Marine Corps birthday cake with son the day he graduates from boot camp

    By David Roza

The innovation unit announced that five companies would move on to the next stage of fielding and testing their vehicles and self-driving systems at Fort Benning and Fort Hood, Texas. Those companies include: Applied Intuition, Forterra/May Mobility, Perrone Robotics, Overland AI/Gatik and Bot Auto.

According to Fort Benning officials, their pilot will have several phases. For the first few weeks, humans will drive cars around base to collect data and video to build out the maps and GPS that fuel the self-driving system’s architecture. Officials noted that driving routes will “explicitly exclude” sensitive facilities like the base airfield, ammunition supply points, and tactical compounds.

Following this so-called “mapping phase,” the companies will run self-driving development and safety tests through the end of 2026.

“Safety remains the overriding priority throughout this pilot,” Auer said. “Before we transition to completely driverless operations, each vehicle will undergo rigorous testing with a safety driver on board.”

Autonomous, self-driving cars are the latest effort to modernize the military’s set of non-tactical vehicles. In 2021, President Biden signed an executive order to replace all federal government vehicles with zero-emission cars, vans and trucks over the next decade. In 2022, the Army released its own climate strategy, which noted that the service had already replaced 18,000 fuel-powered non-tactical vehicles with electric or hybrid versions. 

For the Fort Benning pilot, officials said they plan to bring in four electric and two hybrid vehicles from three of the five private companies.

Forterra, which was chosen for tests at Fort Benning, said in a release that their technology includes a command and control system that gives commanders a live map and dashboard of every vehicle and the ability to adjust parameters and requirements specific to the base. The plan, according to the company, is for soldiers to be able to request a car through a rideshare app. 

According to Forterra, the company has already fielded more than 250 autonomous systems for Defense Department programs, including robotaxis for soldiers at Womack Army Medical Center at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The company also says it was one of the first American companies to deploy ground autonomous systems in Ukraine and has helped with dozens of casualty evacuation missions in the war.

The post The Army is testing self-driving vehicles at bases in Georgia and Texas appeared first on Task & Purpose.

item.title: First female Marine elected to Congress as women veterans hit ‘record’ numbers
item.description:
The former drill instructor served in Iraq and Afghanistan and even did a stint in the Navy. Now she's joining a historic number of women veterans in Congress.

The post First female Marine elected to Congress as women veterans hit ‘record’ numbers appeared first on Task & Purpose.
item.content:encoded:
The first woman to represent the Marine Corps in Congress was just elected to a House seat in Arizona.

JoAnna Mendoza served in the Navy from 1994 to 1997 and the Marine Corps from 1998 to 2016, until she retired as a gunnery sergeant. Mendoza, a Democrat, was just elected to represent Arizona’s 6th Congressional District, which includes the suburbs of Tucson and extends to the southeast part of the state, bordering Mexico.

The first female Marine elected to Congress joins a “record number” of women veterans who will serve when they’re sworn into office in January. The increased number of women elected to Congress, however, comes amid a decline in the overall number of veterans serving, according to an analysis from With Honor Action.

“We’ve seen a decline in veterans serving in Congress, and veterans bring a very unique skill set and experience to really everything. I mean, we’re used to being uncomfortable. We’re used to having difficult conversations and we’re very mission-focused and action-oriented,” Mendoza told Task & Purpose. “About 12 female veterans right now, at least that I’m tracking, I’ll be serving alongside in Congress. It’s a pretty exciting time.”

A dozen women veterans are set to take seats in the House, which would double the number currently serving as federal lawmakers. In the last election, seven female veterans were in the House of Representatives, but it dropped to six after Mikie Sherrill resigned to become governor of New Jersey, according to Seth McCormick Lynn, founder of the Veterans Campaign, a nonpartisan non-profit that educates veterans about civic and political leadership after service.  

“That’s a huge increase, and also a big part because the Democrats have done so well in recent years. Close to half of the new veterans coming out of the Democratic Party into the House have been women,” Lynn said.

Among the women veterans headed to Congress, eight ran as Democrats, and two as Republicans when they won their House seats in November’s midterms. Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral running for a House seat in Colorado, has declared victory in her race against her Republican opponent, but the race had not officially been called as of Tuesday. Those ten women veterans, and Launbacher, are set to join Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), a retired Army Black Hawk pilot, in January.

Lynn said the number of female veterans running for office coincides with more women serving in the military and in public office. He also said what makes these candidates more unique these days is that many of these women serving in Congress post-military service have “impressive military credentials.”

  • News

    By Nicholas Slayton

  • News

    Blue Angels aviator removed from team before homecoming show

    By Nicholas Slayton

  • News

    The Army wants more pilots to apply for its special operations helicopter regiment. Here’s why

    By David Roza

“I think that’s actually kind of the same for a lot of veterans post-9/11. Before that, maybe it was someone who’d done a Reserve gig or time in the National Guard during Vietnam,” he said. “But a lot of them are combat veterans. A lot of them are graduates of service academies. Two coming into office this time are former admirals. It’s an interesting crop.”

Mendoza did tours in Iraq and in Afghanistan and worked as a military administrative specialist, identifying military equipment trends, and deploying with a specialized group in 2012 to Afghanistan to bring back equipment from the Middle East “because we had severely depleted all of our assets on the [Maritime Prepositioning Force] ships,” she said. But Mendoza said, serving as a Marine Corps drill instructor for five years was the “highlight” of her career.

Several veterans who successfully ran as Democrats were part of what election analysts call the “blue wave” and flipped seats held by Republicans. If Laubacher wins, she’ll be joined by Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot who won a New Jersey House seat and Army veteran Cait Conley, who unseated a Republican in New York.

Among the incoming class of veteran congresswomen is Nancy Lacore, a vice admiral who served as chief of the Navy Reserve before she was fired by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in August 2025. She will represent a district in South Carolina. 

“The Democrats are getting a lot of credibility right now to basically do oversight of the Department of War, and that’s going to be an interesting thing to see how they do that,” Lynn said. “It’s a major increase in their ability to do oversight.”

Mendoza said some of the policies she’s interested in working on regarding Iran include safeguarding the military’s stockpile, which has been depleted from ongoing operations, and ensuring the Pentagon’s classification of injuries and casualties in the Iran war is accurate so benefits for military families and veteran benefits aren’t impacted.

“It’s going to be extremely important to have those voices from veterans, from individuals who have served this country and been willing to give their life in service for America and our Constitution, and really push back on this administration, especially when it comes to deploying our troops,” Mendoza said. 

The post First female Marine elected to Congress as women veterans hit ‘record’ numbers appeared first on Task & Purpose.

item.title: Hegseth calls boat strikes ‘lawful’ and ‘successful’ after calls for impeachment
item.description:
Facing the possibility of impeachment, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed that all military actions taken under his watch were legal operations ordered by President Donald Trump.

The post Hegseth calls boat strikes ‘lawful’ and ‘successful’ after calls for impeachment appeared first on Task & Purpose.
item.content:encoded:
Facing the threat of impeachment, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth held a press conference at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where he argued that actions taken under his watch were legal operations ordered by President Donald Trump. 

That includes the ongoing war with Iran; airstrikes against Houthi fighters in Yemen; the raid that captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro; and airstrikes against alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean that have killed at least 240 people.

“Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen: every one was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs,” Hegseth said at a press conference at the Pentagon.

“These are not high crimes,” he added later. “This is the job. And it’s the job well done.”

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, accusing the country’s top civilian defense official of usurping congressional power to wage war, overseeing extrajudicial killings abroad, and attempting to suppress a member of Congress’ freedom of speech.

Top Stories This Week

  • News

    An A-10 named ‘Rainbow Warrior’ sports Marilyn Monroe door art in the Middle East

    By Nicholas Slayton

  • News

    Blue Angels aviator removed from team before homecoming show

    By Nicholas Slayton

  • News

    The Army wants more pilots to apply for its special operations helicopter regiment. Here’s why

    By David Roza

Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment in the House of Representatives. The fifth article, titled “Extrajudicial Killings,” deals with the boat strikes, alleging that Hegseth ordered such strikes without legal authorization from Congress. The administration’s labeling of drug cartels as “designated terrorist organizations” does not authorize the use of military force, the article points out.

U.S. Southern Command has offered little evidence that the boats it struck were engaged in drug trafficking. The Washington Post reported in December that Hegseth’s guidelines required only “reasonable certainty” that a targeted crew member was affiliated with a terrorist organization. That’s a lower threshold than the “near certainty” standard for lethal force against members of Al-Qaeda or similar groups during the Global War on Terror.

Even if the boat crews were members of a group against which military force was authorized, the article argued, the Defense Department allegedly fell short of international laws of armed conflict by reportedly launching a second strike on the survivors of a boat that it had already destroyed. 

“In denying quarter and refusing rescue, Secretary Hegseth endangered members of the United States Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to such treatment,” the article reads.

The United Nations took a similar view when it issued a report in September, arguing that the boat strikes may constitute crimes against humanity.

A confidential assessment by the Drug Enforcement Administration published in July found that the boat strikes have not reduced the amount of cocaine entering the U.S., the Washington Post reported at the time. Fentanyl is the leading cause of illicit drug deaths in the U.S., but it largely enters the country over land, not by sea.

“[This resolution] tells our enemies … that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said Tuesday about the articles of impeachment.

The post Hegseth calls boat strikes ‘lawful’ and ‘successful’ after calls for impeachment appeared first on Task & Purpose.
